b1b-bombers-hasty-departure-england-iran.content:
U.S. Air Force B-1B Lancer bombers have made a hasty departure from RAF Fairford in England, pulling out of the forward base that hosted them during this year's combat operations against Iran after commanders received new intelligence about an Iran-backed threat to the installation.

All 12 of the B-1s stationed at the Gloucestershire airfield left over the weekend, local aircraft spotters and aviation photographers reported, with the jets departing in several waves on Sunday, Oct. 4. A U.S. defense official confirmed the withdrawal to The War Zone, and the Pentagon later acknowledged that every American bomber deployed to Fairford had re-deployed to home stations in the United States. It was the first time in months that the base hosted no U.S. bombers.

## A threat that escalated in hours

The withdrawal was highly unusual for an allied base in a peacetime country thousands of miles from a combat zone. The Times reported that some bombers and their crews departed while aerial refueling tankers were still being scrambled to support the transatlantic flight — a measure of how quickly the order came. At least three of the Lancers had already landed at their home base in South Dakota by Sunday.

According to the Times, commanders acted after receiving new threats about an Iran-backed plot against the installation — warnings that had been building for three weeks before urgency spiked in the previous 24 hours. The Pentagon would not confirm the nature of the intelligence, and the Wall Street Journal was the first to report the departure.

President Donald Trump confirmed on Monday that the threats drove the decision. "They didn't fly out by accident," he told reporters outside the White House. "There were some threats." He added that the United States knew the people behind them. Vice President JD Vance also confirmed the move and accused Iran of plotting attacks against the United States, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio pointed to the "hands of a foreign actor."

## A week of arrests near the base

The evacuation followed a string of arrests around Fairford. On Sept. 27, five men were detained near the base on suspicion of driving vans toward it. Gasoline was found in the vehicles but no explosives, and all five were released on bail. On Oct. 1, a 25-year-old British-Iranian dual national was arrested in London on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts and released on bail; days later, a 22-year-old was arrested in Westminster. No one has been charged.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were strong indications that Iran was behind the suspected plot. Iran denied the accusations, called them baseless, and summoned the British ambassador in Tehran over the matter.

The base was already under a spotlight. Iran had openly threatened Fairford in July, after the airfield's role in strikes on Iranian targets became clear. "Any base that is used to invade Iran's territory is our legitimate goal," Iran's Tasnim News Agency claimed on Telegram on July 23, referring to B-1s flying from Fairford.

## Fairford's role in the Iran campaign

Fairford has been a central hub of the U.S. bomber campaign against Iran. The base hosted a mix of B-1s and B-52s earlier this year, with the total bomber presence at the Gloucestershire hub peaking at 21 to 23 strategic bombers. Six B-52s returned across the Atlantic in a drawdown late last month, leaving about a dozen B-1s — some of which had arrived only days earlier as part of a normal force rotation — to be evacuated.

Stationing bombers at Fairford sharply reduced the flight time needed to reach targets in Iran. The Pentagon emphasized that the withdrawal does not affect readiness.

"The Airmen that operate America's bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s, remain ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities — including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States — anywhere, anytime," the Pentagon said. Both B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s have demonstrated those long-range strikes during this year's operations.

The bombers' repositioning may only be temporary. Fairford remains the U.S. military's forward bomber hub in the United Kingdom — and a fresh reminder that the facilities behind the Iran campaign are themselves in Tehran's sights.

coast-guard-mq9b-drones-248-million.content:
The U.S. Coast Guard has ordered its first MQ-9B drones, buying four of the long-range unmanned aircraft for $247.8 million in a move that gives the maritime service its own persistent airborne eyes for the first time.

The purchase, announced Oct. 9, covers four General Atomics aircraft along with ground control stations and supporting equipment, bought through a U.S. Customs and Border Protection contract. The aircraft are not expected to carry weapons, a service spokesperson told Breaking Defense. They will support offshore surveillance, search-and-rescue operations, and counter-narcotics missions — a broad charter for a service that patrols enormous areas with a relatively small fleet of cutters and aircraft.

## From borrowed drones to its own fleet

The Coast Guard is no stranger to the MQ-9, but until now it has always flown someone else's. The service has partnered with CBP since the mid-2000s to operate the border agency's MQ-9A drones, mostly out of Texas. According to a Coast Guard factsheet, those borrowed aircraft helped CBP seize 60,700 pounds of illegal drugs and catch roughly 20 smugglers in fiscal year 2026 alone.

Owning its own airframes changes the equation. "The MQ-9B long-range unmanned aircraft systems will expand our reach and strengthen our ability to protect the nation," said Anthony Antognoli, the assistant commandant and program executive officer for robotics and autonomous systems, in the Coast Guard's announcement. "This investment will give Coast Guard crews a longer-range view of our maritime domain, helping them detect threats earlier, make better-informed decisions and act faster across our missions."

The funding traces back to the FY25 reconciliation package — the "One Big Beautiful Bill" signed into law in July 2025 — which directed nearly $25 billion to the Coast Guard, along with FY26 appropriations. The service first revealed its MQ-9 plans last year, when Military Times reported that about $266 million of the reconciliation money was earmarked for the drones.

## What four drones buy

The MQ-9B is the long-range variant of the Reaper family, and its numbers explain the Coast Guard's interest. General Atomics says the SeaGuardian version is designed to conduct maritime intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance missions lasting more than 30 hours at a time, with a mission radius of roughly 1,200 nautical miles. For a service whose ships can take days to reach a distant smuggling corridor, that kind of persistence — a single aircraft watching an area for a day and a half, then handing off to a relief crew without missing a beat — is hard to get any other way.

That endurance compares favorably with what the Coast Guard flies today. A Coast Guard C-130 patrols for about 14 hours at a stretch, with a small crew working continuously throughout. With the MQ-9, crews rotate roughly every two hours, keeping a fresh set of eyes on the sensor feed while the aircraft stays on station.

The SeaGuardian variant is purpose-built for over-water work, with maritime radar, automatic identification system receivers, and the ability to dispense and monitor sonobuoys for anti-submarine missions. The Coast Guard did not say whether its aircraft will be the SeaGuardian version, and a service spokesperson did not answer that question, according to Defense Daily.

## A bigger aviation build-up

The drone buy is one piece of a much larger Coast Guard aviation recapitalization. FlightGlobal reported the service also ordered six new C-130J transports as part of a roughly $3 billion effort to modernize its air fleet, with the aircraft positioned as long-range maritime patrol platforms in their own right.

For a service long accustomed to making do with hand-me-downs and borrowed time on other agencies' drones, the MQ-9B order marks a step toward persistent, unmanned surveillance across America's maritime approaches. The drones will detect, classify, and track activity well before it reaches the homeland — giving cutters and boarding teams the one thing they can never get enough of: time.

lockheed-pac3-edge-next-gen-patriot.content:
Lockheed Martin has unveiled the PAC-3 Edge, its next-generation Patriot interceptor — and is backing the missile with hundreds of millions of dollars of its own money before the Army has even settled on the final requirement.

The missile, revealed Oct. 9 just ahead of the Association of the U.S. Army's annual conference, is Lockheed's bid for the Army's Future Interceptor program, which seeks a successor to the current PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement (MSE). Tim Cahill, president of Lockheed's missiles and fire control division, told Breaking Defense the company was one of two firms selected to advance in the program. He declined to name the other competitor, and the Army did not respond to a request for comment.

## What Edge changes

The PAC-3 is the Patriot system's hit-to-kill interceptor, designed to destroy incoming ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and aircraft by slamming into them directly rather than exploding nearby. It has seen real combat in the Middle East and Ukraine, where Patriot batteries have become some of the most valuable — and most heavily targeted — air defense assets in the world.

Edge promises to take that performance further. "PAC-3 Edge will be longer ranged. It'll be higher altitude. It'll be more capable to take on targets that are trying to hide," Cahill said. "It'll have greater sensitivity in its seeker. It'll have greater capability to maneuver and to respond to threats."

The missile pairs a new in-house seeker with a multi-pulse solid rocket motor developed with Northrop Grumman. The seeker was designed by Lockheed's Strigo Product Center, and the company says the motor's pulsed thrust gives the interceptor greater range and altitude throughout its flight than the legacy PAC-3. Control-system upgrades are aimed at delivering that performance against maneuvering targets, including the hypersonic weapons that are stressing current interceptors.

Lockheed plans to begin testing the missile in 2027, with a first deployment targeted for 2031. The company displayed a full-scale model of the weapon at AUSA.

## Lockheed's big bet

The scale of Lockheed's own investment is the real story. The company has already put between $50 million and $100 million into the missile itself, Cahill said — and it intends to spend hundreds of millions more. The seeker effort is bigger still: Lockheed plans to invest about $800 million in the seeker, having already spent "several" hundred million dollars on it, and intends to apply the technology across both offensive and defensive systems.

That confidence is not without a business case. Demand for air defense is at historic highs, driven by conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, and stockpiles are strained. In January, Lockheed signed a seven-year framework agreement with the Pentagon to expand PAC-3 manufacturing capacity from about 600 interceptors a year to 2,000. In July, the Army awarded the company a contract worth up to $58.6 billion to ramp up PAC-3 production, Reuters reported. Cahill told Reuters that the Edge would cost roughly the same as the current PAC-3 MSE, with an annual production rate of about 2,000 units at full production.

Edge would be built on Lockheed's existing PAC-3 line in Camden, Arkansas. The company is building a new MSE production facility there equipped with robotics and advanced manufacturing automation, with production set to move into the new plant — and the legacy facility to receive the same upgrades. "Before we ever get to the point where we're producing Edge, we will have already outfitted the entire factory from end to end with the most modern manufacturing capability available," Cahill said.

## A program that keeps coming back

The Future Interceptor program follows a fits-and-starts effort by the Army to develop a next-generation Patriot interceptor. In 2024, the service announced plans to cancel the Lower-Tier Future Interceptor (LTFI) program, which had seen Raytheon and Lockheed competing to build the new missile. A year later, an Army official suggested the program could move forward after all.

Earlier this year, Lockheed also announced the PAC-3 ACE, a less capable and lower-cost version of the MSE intended for international customers. Edge is the opposite play: the highest-performance interceptor Lockheed can build for the hardest targets the Army expects to face.

hanwha-army-tracked-howitzer-k9.content:
South Korea's Hanwha is not done winning American artillery contracts. Weeks after the Army tapped its wheeled K9 howitzer for a prototype program, the company says it will enter the service's new competition for a tracked variant — offering either its K9A1 or K9A2 self-propelled guns.

"I think it's a must. I mean, when we had early conversations with the Army, we actually thought the Army might be procuring tracked [variants] first," said Mike Smith, Hanwha USA's chief operating officer and president of Land Systems.

## A menu of tracked options

Hanwha USA is looking at a "menu of options" for the tracked competition, Smith said. The K9A1 is the widely fielded and most cost-effective choice, while the newer K9A2 brings more automation and firepower. According to Hanwha, the K9A1 mounts a 155mm, 52-caliber cannon with a range of over 40 kilometers, firing six to eight rounds per minute for three minutes at full capacity.

The K9A2 is the company's next step. It keeps the same drive power as the K9A1 but adds a fully automated turret capable of nine to ten rounds per minute, two independent loading arms for projectiles and propellants, and a new autoloader system that raises the rate of fire while cutting the crew size. Both are members of the K9 Thunder family, one of the most successful artillery systems in the world — in service with South Korea and exported to Poland, Norway, Finland, Australia, Romania, and others.

The Army laid the groundwork for the competition on Sept. 30, when its Program Acquisition Executive for Fires posted a request for information seeking tracked howitzers and a companion resupply vehicle. The solicitation asked vendors about production lead times, maximum production capacity, and strategies for moving production to the United States if their facilities are overseas. An industry day for interested vendors was scheduled for the following week.

Smith suggested Hanwha's existing production lines could shorten the wait: several K9 variants are already in service with land forces around the world. The howitzers are also "completely tailorable," he added — Hanwha can tweak its vehicles to meet the Army's formal requirements.

## The wheeled win that set the stage

Hanwha's bid for the tracked program follows its victory in the wheeled competition, where it beat an unusually crowded field. The Army awarded Hanwha Defense USA a deal worth up to $233 million for the accelerated delivery of six wheeled prototype howitzers, with an option for 12 more. Soldiers will use the prototypes — known as Mobile Tactical Cannon systems — in operational experiments to assess performance, reliability, and supportability in realistic combat conditions.

The losers were a who's-who of global artillery: an Elbit America team with Anduril and Oshkosh Defense offering the SIGMA platform, Leonardo DRS with KNDS and a Caesar-based gun, Germany's Rheinmetall with its Remote Controlled Howitzer 155, and Britain's BAE Systems with Archer.

Hanwha is already laying industrial groundwork in the United States. The company signed a three-year lease on an idle automobile plant in Opelika, Alabama, in April as an integration and test facility for the howitzer program, and Korean media estimate a future mass-production contract — planned for 2027, with initial fielding in 2030 — could reach about 500 guns worth roughly $7.1 billion.

## Why the Army wants both

An Army spokesperson told Breaking Defense the service is pursuing the two variants separately because they "address different operational requirements and formations." The wheeled howitzer is meant to give formations equipped with towed artillery more mobility, survivability, and responsiveness. The tracked variant is intended to keep up with armored formations. Both are aimed at replacing the towed M777 — some of which are 30 to 40 years old — and the self-propelled M109A7, a design first fielded in the 1960s.

The urgency comes from Ukraine, where massed tube artillery has remained decisive even in an age of drones and precision missiles. The Army wants guns that shoot farther, fire faster, and move before enemy counter-battery radar can answer — lessons written in Ukraine that Hanwha's K9, with its automation and rapid-fire rate, was built to deliver.

army-lasers-blast-drones-border-mhel.content:
An Army high-energy laser has shot down three hostile drones near the southern border over two nights in August, in one of the clearest real-world demonstrations yet that directed-energy weapons have moved from the laboratory to the fight.

Service members assigned to Joint Task Force Southern Border — a U.S. Northern Command unit that supports Customs and Border Protection — used the Army's Multi-Purpose High Energy Laser, known as AMP-HEL, to engage and defeat the three drones on Aug. 25 and 26. The aircraft were judged hostile based on their direct support of activity threatening U.S. military personnel and CBP partners, according to the Defense Department, and the footage of the engagements was later released by the Department of War.

## Cartels in the crosshairs

The drones were believed to be linked to Mexican drug cartels, which have made small unmanned aircraft a standard part of their smuggling operations. Cartel networks use cheap quadcopters to scout Border Patrol positions, monitor American personnel, and watch for gaps in border defenses — all without putting an operative physically across the border.

"Cartel networks are increasingly employing unmanned aircraft systems to facilitate illicit human-smuggling and actively spy on our personnel and law enforcement partners," said Army Maj. Gen. Curtis Taylor, commander of Joint Task Force Southern Border. "By integrating layered countermeasures alongside advanced directed-energy capabilities like this laser system, we have made it clear that we will not tolerate hostile surveillance."

The AMP-HEL system was built with directed-energy technology from AeroVironment, and its deployment to the border marks a significant operational milestone. High-energy lasers have been "five years away" for decades, dogged by problems with power, cooling, and keeping a beam steady on a moving target long enough to burn through it. The August engagements suggest those problems are now being solved in the field.

## A surge of incursions

The laser shots came against a backdrop of escalating drone activity. The military detected 378 drone incursions along the southern border in the previous 30 days alone, Brig. Gen. Brian Filler, the task force's deputy commander for operations, told reporters — and the trend is increasing. Most of the aircraft are commercial off-the-shelf models carrying surveillance cameras, often observed flying alongside cross-border smuggling movements.

And the August engagement was not an isolated event. The U.S. military said earlier in October it had downed 11 cartel drones with high-energy lasers since deploying the technology to the border region in August.

The Army has responded by making the desert a proving ground. At Falcon Peak, a Northern Command exercise held in September at Yuma Proving Ground in Arizona, soldiers watched as defense firms demonstrated radars, interceptor drones, autonomous gun systems, and directed-energy weapons designed to detect, track, and destroy small unmanned aircraft. The exercise established permanent counter-drone testing lanes at Yuma — a sign the Army expects the small-drone threat to keep growing.

## Lasers change the cost math

What makes the laser engagements striking is the economics. A cartel drone costs a few hundred or a few thousand dollars. Shooting one down with a missile interceptor costing hundreds of thousands of dollars is a losing trade; dropping one with a beam that costs roughly the price of the fuel running its generator is not. A laser weapon can engage targets repeatedly, at the speed of light, for as long as it has power and a clear line of sight.

That cost exchange is also the military's answer to a lesson from Ukraine, where cheap drones have transformed the battlefield and driven rapid, field-level innovation in both attack and defense. Army planners say they want to reproduce that rapid innovation cycle at home — and the border, with its daily stream of hostile drones, has become their laboratory.

The Army has not said whether the laser will be deployed to the border permanently. But with 11 confirmed kills and hundreds of incursions a month, the case for keeping it there is writing itself.
